summary: Defines a way to frame RTP and RTCP packets over connection-oriented transports such as TCP, and how session descriptions can specify RTP streams that use the framing. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: TCP is a stream with no clear packet boundaries. This adds a small length marker before each real-time packet so the receiver can tell where one ends and the next begins.

questions: how to send rtp over tcp
subtitle: A two-byte length prefix that lets RTP and RTCP packets travel cleanly over TCP, plus an SDP token to announce it.

tldr.problem: TCP delivers a stream of bytes with no packet boundaries, but RTP and RTCP are made of discrete packets. The Audio/Video Profile did not define how to frame them over connection-oriented transport.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet is preceded by a 16-bit LENGTH field in network byte order that equals the packet's size in octets. Session descriptions signal the framing with the new SDP protocol token TCP/RTP/AVP.
tldr.outcome: This documents a framing method that earlier RTP/AVP versions defined and that several implementations already used, and adds SDP signalling for it.

facts.label: Connections per RTP/AVP stream
facts.value: Two (RTP and RTCP) unless b=RS:0 and b=RR:0 are in both offer and answer

today: RFC 4571 is a Proposed Standard and, per the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Framing Is Needed
sections.content:
The Audio/Video Profile (AVP) for the Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550 and RFC 3551) does not define a method for framing RTP and RTCP packets onto connection-oriented transport protocols such as TCP.

Earlier versions of RTP/AVP did define a framing method, and the memo says it is in use in several implementations. RFC 4571 documents that method. It also adds something new: a way for a session description to signal that the framing is used. That signalling was not defined in earlier versions of RTP/AVP.
sections.eli5: Real-time packets are like separate letters, but TCP pours everything out as one stream. This memo explains how to mark where each letter starts and ends.

sections.title: The Framing Method
sections.content:
A frame begins with a LENGTH field: a 16-bit unsigned integer coded in network byte order (big-endian). If LENGTH is non-zero, an RTP or RTCP packet follows it. The value in LENGTH MUST equal the number of octets in that packet. Zero is a valid value and codes the null packet.

The method uses no frame markers, meaning no constant-value octet before LENGTH. Markers help detect errors in LENGTH. Instead, receivers SHOULD monitor RTP and RTCP header fields whose values are predictable, for example the RTP version number. The memo points to Appendix A.1 of RFC 3550 for more guidance.
sections.eli5: Before every packet there is a little note saying how long it is. Without a special start mark, the receiver watches for packets that look wrong to spot a mistake.

sections.title: What the Framing Leaves Open
sections.content:
The framing method is about single packets. It does not specify bi-directional issues (how framed packets in one direction relate to those in the reverse direction), packet loss and reordering, or the RTP and RTCP meaning of closing a TCP socket or any other out-of-band signal.

A reliable connection does not mean a framed RTP stream has contiguous sequence numbers. If the connection tunnels a UDP stream through a middlebox that only passes TCP, the sequence numbers still reflect any loss or reordering on the UDP part of the path. Other memos that normatively include the framing MAY specify these properties.

One property above the single packet is required. If a direction of a connection carries RTP packets, the streams in that direction MUST support multiple synchronization sources (SSRCs). The same rule applies to RTCP packets.
sections.eli5: The memo only says how to wrap each packet. It leaves other questions, like what closing the connection means, to whoever uses it.

sections.title: Signalling with SDP
sections.content:
Session management protocols that use SDP with the Offer/Answer Protocol (RFC 3264) MUST use the methods in COMEDIA (RFC 4145) to set up RTP/AVP streams over TCP, so Offer/Answer is REQUIRED. The memo restricts itself to the Audio/Video Profile and defines the proto token TCP/RTP/AVP for an RTP/AVP stream that uses the framing over TCP. A future profile xyz MUST use the token TCP/RTP/xyz.

The fmt tokens after the proto MUST be unique unsigned integers in the range 0 to 127 and name RTP payload types. Otherwise the syntax matches COMEDIA.

The TCP port on the media line carries RTP. If the stream uses RTCP, a second connection carries it, with its port chosen by the algorithms in SDP or by RFC 3605. Both directions of a connection MUST carry the same type of packet, RTP or RTCP.

Using RTP without RTCP is strongly discouraged. A sender that wants no RTCP adds the lines b=RS:0 and b=RR:0 (from RFC 3556). Only if both offer and answer contain both lines is the RTCP connection skipped. In all other cases endpoints MUST establish two TCP connections, one for RTP and one for RTCP.
sections.eli5: The call description uses a special name, TCP/RTP/AVP, to say 'we send packets over TCP with length tags'. Normally one pipe carries the sound and another carries the status reports.

sections.title: An Example Session
sections.content:
Two session descriptions define a TCP RTP/AVP session. The first party offers m=audio 9 TCP/RTP/AVP 11 with a=setup:active, so it initiates connections. The second uses port 16112, payload types 10 and 11, and a=setup:passive, so it accepts them. Type 11 is stereo L16 and type 10 is mono.

The first party connects to 192.0.2.94 port 16112 and both sides send framed RTP in their own direction of that connection. The first party also opens an RTCP connection to port 16113 (16112 + 1, as defined in SDP) for framed RTCP in both directions.
sections.eli5: One side calls and the other waits. They open one line for the sound and a second line, just next door in port numbers, for status reports.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content: The congestion control requirements for RTP are defined in RFC 3550, and RFC 3551 adds that RTP sessions should compete fairly with TCP flows sharing the network. Because the framing method runs over TCP, it competes fairly with other TCP flows by definition.
sections.eli5: Since the packets ride on TCP, they take turns on the road like other TCP traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors should read the security sections of RFC 3550 and RFC 3551, since most of those issues apply to framed streams. COMEDIA also describes security concerns for connection-oriented media sessions.

The framing adds one risk: attackers may send frames with large LENGTH values to exploit holes in applications. The memo's example is a C program that reads a framed packet into a 1500-byte stack array using LENGTH as the loop bound. An implementation needs to handle every length, from the null packet (LENGTH == 0) to the maximum of 64K octets (LENGTH = 0xFFFF).
sections.eli5: A bad sender could claim a huge packet to overflow a small box. Programs must be ready for any size from nothing to the biggest the tag can say.
